I would like to use the "time" column as the x value. Other columns are y values of points in different lines. In the data above, there are 4 lines, each line consists of 5 points. More specifically, the first line has points (200, 17230622635), (400, 22328386154), (600, 28958840968), etc. The second line has points (200, 17280401147), (400, 22456712709), etc. (If you need further explanation of the data format, see P.S. in the end.)

To generate a similar data, you could use the following code:

    rs = data.frame(seq(200, 1000, by=200), runif(5), runif(5), runif(5))
    names(rs)=c("time", 1:3)

I followed some examples on stack overflow and tried to use reshape2 and ggplot2 to do this plot:

I first melt the data into a "long-format":

    library('reshape2')
    library('ggplot2')
    melted = melt(rs, id.vars="time")

Then plot the data using the following statment:

    ggplot() + geom_line(data=melted, aes(x="time", y="value", group="variable"))

However, I got an empty graph which has no point nor line.

Can anyone help me to see what's wrong with my procedure? Thank you in advance!

Regards,
-Nan

You can imagine there are many students in the class and we have their scores of several quizzes. messages.subject_clean: how to plot 2 sets on one graph
messages.body_plain:
If you 2 (or more) y values share a meaningful common scale then you
can use the matplot function to create the multiple plots.

 If they don't share a common scale then they should not be on the
same plot, it is better to plot them in 2 plots (close together is
fine) aligned vertically.  When multiple sets are plotted together
then the eye is drawn to points where lines (or patterns) cross, when
the scales are different then these crossings are a result of
arbitrary choices in scaling rather than anything meaningful from the
data.

messages.body_plain:
The argument expand =  in scale_*_continuous() controls the padding;
setting expand = c(0, 0) removes it. If you don't want points, don't
use geom_point(). Here's the simplest way I know of to reproduce your
plot sans the point:

nofly <- data.frame(x=c(-1, -1, 3, 3, -1, -1, 3, 3),
                    y=c(-1, 0, 0, -1, 1, 2, 2, 1),
                    id=rep(1:2, each=4))

library(ggplot2)
ggplot() +

    geom_polygon(data=nofly, fill="red", alpha=0.3,

                 aes(x = x, y = y, group=id)) +
    scale_y_continuous("Probability", expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
    geom_abline(intercept=0.2, slope=0.8, size = 1)

The aesthetics you want are in nofly, so you can define them in the
geom_polygon() layer. It is legitimate to pass an empty argument list
to ggplot(), which will set up an empty base layer. Since
geom_abline() doesn't explicitly need a data frame when the intercept
and slope are vectors of length 1 (i.e., they are set rather than
mapped), you have everything you need. All I did was add a size
argument to geom_abline() to make it a bit thicker.

The following also works because geom_abline() doesn't use any of the
aesthetics defined in the ggplot() call and only one data frame is in
play:

ggplot(data=nofly, aes(x = x, y = y, group=id)) +
    geom_polygon( fill="red", alpha=0.3) +
    scale_y_continuous("Probability", expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
    geom_abline(intercept=0.2, slope=0.8, size = 1)

Dennis

On 2014-05-02 10:38 PM, Matthew Sundquist wrote:
> Sorry for being slow! This went into the wrong folder.

>
> Plotly in this case is meant to be a sharing, collaboration, and
> visualization layer. Like what GitHub is for sharing and collaborating
> on code, we'd love to do for sharing and collaborating on data and plots.

This is helpful but I am still not clear on where various pieces of data
and code are *stored*.

Github is unusual in (so far) maintaining its existence and
independence; the track record of similar collaboration services is not
good.  They typically have a lifetime of less than five years, after
which they go out of business entirely, are purchased and shut down, or
reinvent themselves as something which does not serve their original
function.  As such, in a scientific context I am only okay with using
them for secondary functions -- not the core function of preserving my
data and results long-term.

What this means for your project is:  I'm only interested in using it if
*all of my data* and *all of the essential code to produce the plots*
can be stored on a server that I (or some entity that I trust to remain
in existence long-term) control.  Essential code means code that, if it
went away, the plots would disappear or lose basic interactivity.  It is
okay if the sharing-and-remixing part depends on an external service,
because that is a secondary function -- in principle someone could just
grab the raw data, do what they want with it, and put it up on their own
host.  (It would be *better* if the sharing-and-remixing didn't depend
on an external service, but I recognize that that's a tall order in
today's Web.)

messages.body_plain:
I am attempting to use ggplot2 to create a map of the 50 US states with Alaska and Hawaii as insets. After talking with members of the GIS community they recommended this method (insets) as opposed to modifying the shapefile to "move" AK and HI to the desired locations.  It appears that ggplot2 supports insets via the annotation_custom <http://docs.ggplot2.org/0.9.3.1/annotation_custom.html> function.  However, I am finding that ggplot2 will only render one of my insets, and it's always the one I write first.

I am attaching the shapefiles and R code as attachments. I am also attaching screenshots.  Note that in my screenshots the grobs for AK and HI only show the axes, and AK is placed incorrectly - this is just because I am reproing the bug and removed some excess code that that prettified the image.

For reference, I created a github repo  <https://github.com/arilamstein/choroplethr-maps>for my shapefile which explains where I got it from as well as the modifications I made for it.

Here is my code which reproduces the bug.  Am I using annotation_custom correctly?  Is there a bug in ggplot2 related to this particular situation?  Is there another way for me to accomplish what I am trying to do?

Thanks.

Ari

require("rgdal") # requires sp, will use proj.4 if installed
require("maptools")
require("ggplot2")
require("plyr")
require(gpcilb)
gpclibPermit()

# the smallest of the state shapefiles
setwd("~/R/choroplethr-maps/state")

# get the shapefile as a data.frame
us.states = readOGR(dsn=".", layer="gz_2010_us_040_00_20m")
us.states@data$id = rownames(us.states@data)
us.states.points = fortify(us.states, region="id")
us.states.df = join(us.states.points, us.states@data, by="id")

# separate contiguous states from Alaska and Hawaii
us.states.48 = us.states.df[!us.states.df$NAME %in% c("Alaska", "Hawaii"), ]
alaska.df = us.states.df[us.states.df$NAME=='Alaska',]
hawaii.df = us.states.df[us.states.df$NAME=='Hawaii',]

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I never rely on positional arguments for anything serious, but the following got me thinking:

reg_fn_sq <- function(x) (x - .5)^2
ggplot(data.frame(x = seq(0, 1, by = .1)), aes(x)) + stat_function(reg_fn_sq)

reg_fn_sq is matched to the 'mapping' above, because mapping is the first argument to stat_function. I imagine that the reason that mapping is the first argument is because mapping is the first argument to many geoms and stats. I respect consistency but it seems a little strange because I don't think many people are going to override the general mapping very often. But everyone who uses stat_function will need to give it a function argument. Most of the help examples are just passing only the function argument, sometimes with a color or argument list.

For the sake of argument, I want to take the position that positional matching should be encouraged and have sensible defaults for the special case where the function is called with one argument. Also for the sake of argument, I want to say that this should take precedence over consistency. Why? Because the consistency or ordering argument names only comes into play when users rely on positional arguments for multiple arguments, which should not be encouraged.

As you can see by my two "for the sake of argument" statements, I'm not yet convinced by my reasoning. Just curious.

Any thoughts on this?

Best,

Scott

least one end of the missing error bars are outside that range. By
default, data outside the axis range is dropped, and if part of the
error bar is dropped, then none of it can be drawn.

data. Search for discussion of "dynamite plots" for further reading

It's not really clear what you want. Here is an example where I take theme_bw() and change a few parameters in it.

#### Theme for inset plot, reduces all unnecessary space and just prints the plot
theme_inset <- function (base_size = 12, base_family = ""){
  theme_bw (base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) %+replace%
     theme(
    axis.line = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(0.3)),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.5)),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.length = unit(0, "lines"),
    axis.ticks.margin = unit(0, "lines"),
    legend.position = "none",
    #panel.background = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_blank(),
    #panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.margin = unit(0, "lines"),
    plot.background = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = unit(c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), "lines"),
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_blank()
    )
  }

To use it, you just add it to your ggplot() call like any other theme.
Using your example:

# here is my "theme-less" code:
ggplot(MYDATA, aes(year,VARIABLE,colour=factor(Type)))+
  geom_line(size=1,linetype=c(1))
  scale_color_manual(name  ="MY LEGEND",
                    values=c("1","2"),
                    labels=c("47", "50") )   +
  labs(x = "", y = "") +

  facet_wrap(~LEVELS, ncol=2)+
theme_inset()

HTH, B

messages.subject: graphical depiction of effect sizes
messages.body_plain:
Not really about ggplot, but I'm hoping the folks on this list may have
some ideas.  Plus, if there is a way to do it with ggplot I'd love to know.

We have estimated effects of variables on each other, both direct and
indirect effects.  This is usually presented graphically with a bunch of
boxes representing variables and arrows representing effects.  The
effect size and sometimes the uncertainty interval is presented as text
above the relevant line.  Here's an ascii art version:
_____        0.4 (0.2, 0.6)  ______
|  A   | ---------------------> |   B    |
=====                                ======

meaning the effect of A on B is .4 with a confidence interval from 0.2
to 0.6.  The real diagram has a lot more boxes and effects, and includes
direct and indirect effect.  Often this is handled by putting the total
effect above the line and the direct effect below it.

I would like to present this graphically, probably by making the
thickness of the line proportional to the effect size, with a shaded
cloud around it indicating uncertainty.

There are a number of challenges:
* Effect sizes vary widely, from 0.5 to essentially 0.  I would like
0.01 to be visually distinguishable from 0.03.  Even with the
uncertainty intervals, I think most of the action is under 10%.
* If the effect is 0.4 and it ranged from -0.02 to 0.10 it is easy
enough to show the cloud of uncertainty using fainter colors (e.g.,
lower opacity).  But if the lower limit is positive (as in the ascii
graph above) it is less clear to me how to present it.
* It would be useful to use color, e.g., positive effects are black and
negative ones are red), but we may be limited to black and white for
publication.
* Presenting total and direct effect information in the same arrow seems
liable to produce information overload.

Any ideas?

Thanks.
Ross Boylan

messages.body_plain:
Here's a hack solution that overwrites white lines on the existing
plot. The following is what is known as a "reproducible example",
which includes both code and *data*.

library(ggplot2)

# Generate some fake mixture data
DF <- data.frame(grp = factor(rep(c("Good", "Poor"), each = 1000),
                              levels = c("Poor", "Good")),
                 y = c(rnorm(250, 13, 2), rnorm(750, 15, 0.5),
                       rnorm(750, 13, 1), rnorm(250, 15, 0.5)))
# Truncate the upper bound at 16
DF$y <- pmin(DF$y, 16)

ggplot(DF, aes(x = y, color = grp)) + geom_density() +
   geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "white") +
   geom_vline(xintercept = 16, color = "white") +
   scale_color_manual("Custom\n   title", values = c("darkorange", "blue"))

Note the following:

1. The two geoms that add the horizontal and vertical lines come
*after* geom_density().
2. This should cover your question about legend titles.
3. Overwriting the x-axis may obscure part of the density plot if the
density is sufficiently small over a localized region.

I noticed that you had thicker lines for the density curves. To
accommodate this, I increased the size of the hline and vline as well
as the major axis lines correspondingly - otherwise you'll get
partially uncovered h/vlines:

ggplot(DF, aes(x = y, color = grp)) + geom_density(size = 1) +
   geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "white", size = 1) +
   geom_vline(xintercept = 16, color = "white", size = 1) +
   scale_color_manual("Custom\n  title", values = c("darkorange", "blue")) +
   theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(size = 1))

FYI, the red was changed to dark orange to help out our red-green
color blind friends.

Dennis

These are my suggestions from a graphics practice perspective, because graphics is important for displaying effect size.

The TikZ example is ineffective. You need to have a meaningful mapping of numerical value to graphical element. Mapping to line width is very inaccurate, see Cleveland's hierarchy of visual elements. This display no better than showing a table of the numbers.

It is important to show the data, particularly when displaying effect size. My main experience is from bioinformatics examples, where there is massive multiple testing.  In bioinformatics, fold change is a popular statistic, and a measure of effect size, but on its own it is misleading. Ideally one pots the data, on a relevant scale to all the data used, along with other indicators of fold change and statistical significance. Similarly just showing p-values, even adjusted p-values, for bioinformatics is also misleading. They should be accompanied by plots of the data and the fold change.

messages.subject: Re: Ends of Density Plot
messages.body_plain:
The wraparound is just the way it's defined to be drawn in ggplot2
using geom_density(); I suspect the intention was to easily
accommodate fill colors, particularly when multiple density estimates
are compared in a single graphics panel. One alternative is to use the
stat_density() function instead and use a different geom to render it,
such as geom_path(). Here's a revised (and much less hackish) version
of my previous example:

DF <- data.frame(grp = factor(rep(c("Good", "Poor"), each = 1000),
                              levels = c("Poor", "Good")),
                 y = c(rnorm(250, 13, 2), rnorm(750, 15, 0.5),
                       rnorm(750, 13, 1), rnorm(250, 15, 0.5)))
# Truncate the upper bound at 16
DF$y <- pmin(DF$y, 16)

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(DF, aes(x = y, color = grp)) +

   stat_density(aes(y = ..density..), geom = "path", size = 1) +

   scale_color_manual("Custom\n   title", values = c("darkorange", "blue"))

That should address your present concern.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

You have a few things wrong in your code:

1. The input data frame to ggplot() should be precip, not prec.
2. Per your code, the object precip$TIMESTAMP is a factor, not a
POSIXct object, which is what you need to enable date-time formats in
ggplot2.
3. In order to use scale_x_datetime(), the scales package must be
loaded first (as of at least ggplot2-0.9.0, released in 2012).

The first step is to create the proper date-time format in the data
frame. I do this in two steps because, for some reason, if I compose
the function calls into one statement, the local time zone is
retained, which we don't really need here. Add the following lines to
your code after precip is defined and before invoking ggplot():

library(scales)

# Conversions: factor -> character -> POSIXlt
precip$time <- strptime(as.character(precip$TIMESTAMP),
                  format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")

# Convert from POSIXlt to POSIXct
precip$time <- as.POSIXct(precip$time)

As noted by Rajesh, it's also a good idea to add the theme function
early in the call, so this should get what you wanted:

ggplot(precip, aes(x=time, y=Rain_mm_1_Tot)) +
  theme_bw() +

  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="dodge") +
  scale_x_datetime(breaks = "1 week", labels = date_format("%D"),
                   expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,2)) +
  labs(title = "Daily Precipitation", x="Date", y="Precipitation (mm)") +
  facet_grid(source ~ .) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=60, hjust = 1))

However, I'm not a big fan of angled text; I prefer either a different
presentation format or a coord_flip() when the strings are
sufficiently long. Here's one alternative date format among several
that could be applied without string rotation:

ggplot(precip, aes(x=time, y=Rain_mm_1_Tot)) +
  theme_bw() +

  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="dodge") +

  scale_x_datetime(breaks = "1 week", labels = date_format("%b\n%d"),

                   expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,2)) +
  labs(title = "Daily Precipitation", x="Date", y="Precipitation (mm)") +
  facet_grid(source ~ .)

I would be prone to add a line to either the plot title or a figure
caption to define the range of dates that the graph spans since the
year is the same in this graph. Alternatively, you could use the
x-axis label "2014 dates". With multiple year spans, there are other
ways to format dates.

It's also not clear to me why you need position = "dodge" in
geom_bar() since you have no grouping factor defined. Taking it out
produces some warnings about missing values, but I don't see any
visual difference in the plots with and without position = "dodge"
(but I could be neglecting something).
